title: Common ground + name fight over calling remote-disposing faith saving
source_text: XXXVI. Porro, ut clarum est ex iis quae dicta sunt, Theologi Scholae Reformatae Ecclesiae Romanae Doctoribus concedunt, esse quandam fidem, quae sit Spiritus Sancti donum, & per quam aliquis reipsa Dei Verbo assentitur, quae tamen juncta non est cum charitate & bonis operibus; & in multis improbis hominibus reperitur. Consentiunt etiam utriusque Scholae Doctores, ejusmodi fidem actu neminem servare & justificare; neque negabunt Reformati illam esse quandam remotam ad salutem praeparationem. Quaestio solummodo est, an propterea quod remote ad justitiam & salutem disponat, illi tribui debeat nomen salvificae & justificantis, & nomen verae fidei; quia vero objecto, Spiritu Sancto movente, revera assentitur, quamvis de caetero credenti maneat inutilis. Quae quaestio, ut apparet, de nomine tantum est, cum de re ipsa constet. Quanquam rationi, & Scripturae stylo congruentius sit, eam solum fidem justificantem & salvificam vocare, quae actu servat atque salvificat, non vero eam quae actu & reipsa ad justitiam & salutem habentis nihil prodest. Ut & verae fidei nomen merito appropriari potest, illi quae finem suum assequitur, & per quam aliquis credit bene & sicut oportet. Praesertim cum saepe Scriptura fidem simpliciter nominans, ejusmodi fidem, & non aliam intelligat.
pass_a_gloss: Moreover, as is clear from what has been said, Reformed-school theologians concede to Roman Doctors that there is a certain faith which is a gift of the Holy Spirit and by which someone really assents to God's Word, which yet is not joined with charity and good works, and is found in many wicked men. Doctors of both schools also agree that such faith actually saves and justifies no one; nor will the Reformed deny that it is a certain remote preparation for salvation. The question only is whether, because it remotely disposes to righteousness and salvation, the name of saving and justifying, and the name of true faith, ought to be attributed to it — because it really assents to a true object by the Holy Spirit moving, although otherwise it remains useless to the believer. Which question, as appears, is only about the name, since the thing itself is settled. Although it is more congruent with reason and Scripture's style to call only that faith justifying and saving which actually saves, not that which actually and in reality profits nothing for the holder's righteousness and salvation. So also the name of true faith can deservedly be appropriated to that which attains its end and by which someone believes well and as one ought — especially since Scripture often naming faith simply understands such faith and no other.
pass_b_english: Both sides: Spirit-gifted assent without charity exists in the wicked and actually saves no one; Reformed allow remote preparation.
Name-fight: should remote-disposing faith be called true/saving? Better style reserves those names for faith that actually saves.
